segments: If you clicked on this video, you probably know who Rick Clips is.
His AI videos get at least a million views every day.
And in this video, I'll show you how to make videos that come genuinely close to his quality.
Before you write me off as another YouTube guru who promises Rick-level videos and delivers
nothing close, let me show you the results. Here's a video I made myself.
And here's a side-by-side comparison. I'll walk you through how I achieve this quality
and how you can make these videos yourself. I've also built tools into the skill that let you
shape the video exactly the way you want it. So stay until the end.
So what's the real difference between my videos and everyone else's?
Let's start with the characters. Most creators rely on character sheets,
which are sets of pre-drawn poses of the character. Because of that, every movement is limited,
and I'll show you exactly what that means shortly.
Their characters are also usually a single flat color. The entire face is one solid fill,
which is what makes it look flat. Now look at mine. The face is pure white,
with cell shading on one side and a small highlight along the edge.
That shading isn't fixed in one spot. It follows the light source in the scene.
So if the light moves or the character turns, the shading moves with it.
That's what keeps the character from looking flat.
Next, expressions. Others use a fixed set of faces. One for happy, one for sad, one for angry,
and that's it. This gives the character limited expressions, and it shows.
My approach is different. I give Claude reference faces to work from, but it isn't restricted to
them. Claude draws every expression based on what the character is feeling in that exact moment.
It can even blend emotions, like slightly surprised and slightly worried at the same time,
which produces expressions that don't exist in the references at all.
When the emotion changes, the face doesn't snap from one expression to the next. It transitions
across several frames. The eyebrows move first, and the mouth follows. If the eyes need to change
shape, the switch is hidden inside a blink, and the head adds a small bounce so the change feels
natural. Now, clothes and accessories. In most videos, the clothing either always faces the
camera or flips abruptly from one angle to another when the character turns. Here's how I handle it.
The body shape always faces the camera, but the clothing is drawn as if it's wrapped around a
round invisible form underneath. When the character turns, the clothes turn with them. The stripes,
buttons, tie, and pockets shift toward the side and compress near the edge, just like real clothing
on a real body. The clothing is also lit by the same light as the rest of the scene. One side is
slightly brighter, and the other slightly darker, with a soft sheen, a thin highlight along the
edge where the light hits, and subtle fold lines where the fabric would bunch up. If something
casts a shadow on the character, like a tree or a roof, that shadow falls across the clothing too.
Accessories follow the same logic. Hats and hair are redrawn every frame to match the tilt of the
head, so they lean and rotate with it, and they get their own highlights. When a character holds
something, like a saw or a steering wheel, that object exists as a real 3D object in the scene,
and the hands land on it and grip it. Then, character movement. Others use character sheets
for movement as well, and that creates the same limitations. The character is almost always standing,
the legs stay straight, and the only poses available are the ones that were drawn,
so it can't convincingly meal, sit, crouch, or pick something up. My approach is built around
how the arms, legs, and body are animated. Every character has an underlying 3D skeleton,
with hips, chest, head, knees, elbows, hands, and feet. That skeleton moves through 3D space like
a real body. The feet stay planted where they step, so there's no sliding. The knees and
elbows bend the way real joints do, and the hands reach the actual objects they're interacting with.
On top of that skeleton, the character is drawn in 2D, fresh, on every single frame. The body,
arms, legs, clothing, face, and hat are all redrawn to match the pose for that exact frame.
That means the character can do almost anything. Kneel down to cut the road,
sit in a car with bent knees and hands on the wheel, jump, fall, or swing a hammer,
all while still looking like a clean 2D cartoon. Next, backgrounds and objects. Other creators use
3D backgrounds too, but they're mostly flat colors with no texture and very simple shapes.
In my videos, the whole world is real 3D, and Claude builds every single thing in it from code.
Nothing is downloaded or pasted in. The road, the guardrails, the fields, the cars, the signs,
the saw, even the coffee thermos. All of it is built from scratch.
Because Claude builds each object part by part, every part can move on its own.
Cardoors open to reveal a real interior, with seats, pedals, a dashboard, and thick door panels.
The wheels turn. A guardrail bends when a car hits it. The saw's blade spins.
Everything has texture too. The road has cracks and small stones. The seats have stitching.
The sign has dirt and bolts on it, and the fields stretch all the way to the horizon.
The world also reacts to the story. When he cuts the road, real grooves appear, along with sparks
and dust. When a car crashes, the rail bends. The car gets dented and the camera shakes.
Now, lighting. Most creators use flat lighting, where everything is equally bright and there
barely any shadows. In my videos, there's a real sun in the sky, and everything gets its light from
it. Objects cast real shadows on the ground, and clouds cast soft shadows that drift across the
fields. Shiny objects like the cars, the saw, and the hard hat catch the light with small highlights.
The scene also moves through time of day. Day turns into sunset, and sunset turns into a dark
night, where the headlights light up the road and everything around them stays dark.
Here's the key part. The characters are lit by that same sun. Their shading and
highlights follow wherever the light is coming from, so they always look like they belong in the
scene. Even at night, their faces stay white and clean instead of turning muddy gray. And if something
casts a shadow on a character, like a tree or a roof, that shadow lands on them too. Finally,
camera and sound effects. The camera always follows the story. Whenever the voice talks
about an object or something the character is doing, the camera smoothly zooms in on it,
like the saw cutting the road or the coffee spilling on the seat, and then eases back out.
Every move is slow and smooth, with no sudden jumps. It also uses creative angles, right down at
road level next to the grooves, high up looking down the highway, through the car's side window,
and from the driver's own point of view. For sound, every effect is a real recording placed
on the exact moment it happens on screen. You hear the saw when it cuts, cars driving past,
the crunch when a car hits the rail, and the splash when the coffee goes everywhere.
None of these sounds are generated by Claude. It downloads them straight from the internet,
which is what makes them sound so realistic. The background music sits under the voice,
loud enough to set the mood without covering what's being said.
Now, when I have a video script, I plan every scene in full detail before anything gets made.
That includes the camera moves, the angles, what each character does, and what happens on every
line of the voice, because AI is only as smart as the person prompting it. If you want to skip
the hard part and start making quality videos right away, the skill is available in my school
community. It includes a guide on how to write your prompts so you get exactly the video you want.
It also comes with two tools. The first is a camera editor, where you can change the camera
moves and angles in your video. The second is a background music picker, where you watch the
fully rendered video, try different tracks over it, and pick the one that fits best.
And no, it's not free. I can't realistically help everyone who reaches out if it is,
and I've put a lot of time and effort into getting it to this level of quality.
That's all for today. Make sure to like and subscribe. See you in the next one!
